newsitem.title: JAPAN: TIFFE Euroyen futures higher on stocks tumble.
newsitem.headline: TIFFE Euroyen futures higher on stocks tumble.

text.p: Key March three-month Euroyen deposit rate futures were fed by tumble of Tokyo stocks in the afternoon on Friday.
Dealers said the market lacked factors of its own and was looking at other markets throughout the session.
In the morning, the March took direction from a fall of the Japanese government bond futures, but it rebounded after the market found support at 99.14 unbreakable.
The sharp drop in the Nikkei stock index in the afternoon prompted those who went short to cover their positions, dealers said.
The March contract moved in a range of between 99.18 and 99.14. Many dealers said 99.20 is a major resistance, the level which blocked the contract on Thursday.
Turnover was 33,966 contracts. Dealers said trade was thin before a three-day weekend. The market will be closed on Monday due to a national holiday.
The market is looking to the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting in the United States, due on Tuesday.

Although opinions are divided on whether the Fed will raise rates, many dealers said the impact of the FOMC will be limited, as the Bank of Japan's (BOJ) monetary policy is unlikely to change whatever the Fed does.

In the interbank call market, the majority of key overnight call money was traded at 0.47 percent, down 0.01 from Thursday. The BOJ's market operation this morning was neutral as expected. Traders said there was a tug-of-war between upward pressure coming from fund demand due to bond settlements and downward pressure due to the so-called weekend factor -- fund raisers' tendency to wait until the rate falls.
In the open market, about 30 billion yen worth of key three-month certificates of deposit (CDs) were issued at 0.53 percent, the same rate as Thursday.
About 20 billion yen worth of two-month CDs were issued at an unchanged 0.52 percent. One-month CDs were offered at the same level.
One trader at a long-term credit bank said those rates are likely to be stable for the time being.
But these rates might be inclined to go down after the end of September, as fund demand related to many Japanese firms' half-year book-closings will ebb, the trader added.
